chapter: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
title: Billy Douglas sits in with Roy Eldridge and Dizzy Gillespie
summary: At a Sunday jam session Douglas ran all the chords and impressed Roy Eldridge and the others.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Well, you know, there's -- Earl made some records about '40 -- oh, '46 or '47, and there's a couple of solos on those records, and a lot of people thought they were by Willie Cook, but Earl listened to them, and he told me they were by Billy Douglas. And he sort of (unintelligible).

Oh, he could play some beautiful chords. I [bought] -- when I left Philadelphia -- see, we go up to New York and visit. Came up wanted to visit a girlfriend of mine, and so -- okay, this place called a Hut. (Louis Metcalf had a (unintelligible) place on 145th Street where we all used to jam. So I called Louis (unintelligible), said, come on, Hap, says, glad to see you, because we were both writing for the Music Dial. And I said, Billy, let's go down

Billy always carried his horn with him. He would never go anywhere without that horn. I said, look here, I said, 'I'm not going to take my horn,' I said. 'Let's go over and have some fun with the guys.' So Roy Eldridge, Dizzy Gillespie, all of the bunch there playing on a Sunday, and they were jamming. So Billy was concerned -- (unintelligible) said, hey, Hap, he said. Hey, what are you doing, I said. Want you to introduce to a friend of mine, Billy Douglas. Yes, he said, he knows Billy because Billy worked at the Savoy with different little groups.

So right then Billy, said, (unintelligible) you got your horn, said, come on and sit in. Well, they're playing them -- [nice] tempo, you know. Said, well, Roy didn't know that this boy had good execution, see, and he run all them chords. See, he got that -- (unintelligible) Benny got it from him.

From Billy Douglas. See, but what happened. Billy didn't get it from him to give to (unintelligible), but Billy followed him, because Cuban was the first one came around with all them chords on the trumpet. That was Benny Carter's cousin.
So they took a (unintelligible) right after Cuban Bennett, and Billy was a very good musician, and

so consequently he could write, (unintelligible) That was up Billy's alley. So they were playing this fast two/four. Billy always sit down (unintelligible) and crossed his legs and (unintelligible) play like nothing ever happened. So when he got to these chords, Roy was running, you know, and when Billy got to it, everybody sat there and listened. He ran over all those chords, didn't miss no chords and (unintelligible) run the music. Where in the hell did that guy come from? I said, he's been in New York before. He's been in Philadelphia (unintelligible) for quite a few years, said, he's out of Connecticut.
Said, what? I said, sure. So, cheese and crackers, mister, he's sort of like Cuba Kewpie Bennett. I said (unintelligible).
